title: A Little-Known Trait Every Teacher Needs
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes an under-discussed trait he calls awareness, the ability to stay present and alert in the classroom, as a differentiator between struggling and highly effective teachers. He offers four practical guidelines for cultivating it: talking less to sharpen perception and impact, slowing down to read the room accurately, maintaining an observational mindset at all times rather than only during independent work, and breathing fully to counter the physiological narrowing that comes with stress. He connects a lack of awareness to a broader lack of teaching wisdom, arguing that scatterbrained, rushed teachers invite students to test and take advantage of them regardless of intelligence or preparation. The article frames awareness as a learnable skill rather than an innate gift.
points: Names 'awareness' — the ability to stay present and alert — as a rarely discussed trait shared by the most effective teachers.
Recommends cutting talking by about a third, arguing that excessive talk causes students to tune teachers out.
Advises slowing physical pace and speech to sharpen perception of classroom tone, strengths, and energy levels.
Urges maintaining an observational mindset at all times, not only during independent work, to protect safety and consistency.
Connects shallow, stressed breathing to narrowed vision and diminished teaching presence, and recommends full breathing as a corrective.
quotes: Most teachers would benefit by cutting the amount of talking they do by one-third. Because talking too much causes students to tune you out.
By taking your time, by waiting, pausing, and moving more deliberately, your senses are better able to tune into the tone and temperature of your classroom.
It isn’t just important during periods of independent work. It’s important to have an observational mindset all the time .
When you’re stressed out, anxious, or worried, your breathing shallows. Your vision narrows. Your senses constrict.
Teachers who rush around, talk a lot, have narrow vision, and breathe in short, shallow breaths appear as if they don’t have their wits about them.
For many teachers, improving this one area is the missing ingredient. It’s the reason why they’ve felt as if nothing they do works as promised.
